activities.title: Practical Context: Self-Balancing Radar Range Scanning

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Self-Balancing Radar Range Scanning
analogy.story:
In aviation flight control systems, radar tracks hundreds of aircraft at varying altitudes. Air traffic controllers do not just ask 'Is plane X airborne?'; they ask range queries: 'What is the closest plane strictly above 10,000 feet?' and 'Give me all aircraft flying between 5,000 and 15,000 feet.'

A hash table cannot answer range questions efficiently because hashes scatter data randomly across buckets. A self-balancing search tree arranges all targets in strict sorted order, allowing controllers to locate boundary limits and range slices in logarithmic O(log N) time.
analogy.keyTakeaway: TreeSet trades O(1) hash speed for O(log N) sorted tree navigation. It excels at boundary queries, proximity lookups, and range slicing.

activities.title: TreeSet Architecture: Red-Black Trees & The NavigableSet Contract

keyTakeaways: TreeSet implements NavigableSet and SortedSet, backed internally by a java.util.TreeMap
Elements are stored in a self-balancing Red-Black binary search tree with O(log N) guarantees
TreeSet requires elements to implement Comparable or requires a custom Comparator in its constructor
TreeSet does NOT use equals() or hashCode() to determine element uniqueness; it relies strictly on compareTo() or compare() == 0

activities.content:
### Definition of TreeSet & Red-Black Tree Architecture

A **`TreeSet<E>`** is a sorted collection implementing the `NavigableSet<E>` and `SortedSet<E>` interfaces, backed internally by a **`java.util.TreeMap`**. Elements are maintained in total sorted order using either their natural ordering (`java.lang.Comparable`) or an explicit `java.util.Comparator` provided at instantiation.

The underlying data structure is a self-balancing **Red-Black Tree**, which guarantees $O(\log N)$ time complexity for basic operations (`add`, `remove`, `contains`):
* Every node is either red or black.
* The root is always black.
* No two consecutive red nodes are permitted (a red node cannot have a red child).
* Every path from root to leaf contains the exact same number of black nodes (black height).
These invariants ensure the tree height never exceeds $2 \log_2(N + 1)$, preventing degenerating into an $O(N)$ linked chain.

---

### The NavigableSet Boundary API & Range Operations

Unlike `HashSet`, `TreeSet` exposes rich range navigation operations:
* **`first()` / `last()`**: Returns the lowest / highest element in the set.
* **`floor(e)` / `ceiling(e)`**: Returns the greatest element $\le e$, or lowest element $\ge e$ (inclusive).
* **`lower(e)` / `higher(e)`**: Returns the greatest element $< e$, or lowest element $> e$ (strictly exclusive).
* **`subSet(from, to)`**: Returns a dynamic view of elements between `from` and `to`.
* **`descendingSet()`**: Returns a reverse-order view in $O(1)$ time.

---

### Executable Demonstration: Proximity Lookups with TreeSet

```java
import java.util.NavigableSet;
import java.util.TreeSet;

public class TreeSetNavigationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NavigableSet<Integer> stockPrices = new TreeSet<>();
        stockPrices.add(105);
        stockPrices.add(120);
        stockPrices.add(150);
        stockPrices.add(180);
        stockPrices.add(210);

        System.out.println("Sorted Prices: " + stockPrices);
        System.out.println("First (Min):   " + stockPrices.first());
        System.out.println("Last (Max):    " + stockPrices.last());

        // Boundary queries
        System.out.println("Ceiling >= 140: " + stockPrices.ceiling(140)); // 150
        System.out.println("Floor <= 140:   " + stockPrices.floor(140));   // 120
        System.out.println("Higher > 150:   " + stockPrices.higher(150));  // 180
        System.out.println("Lower < 150:    " + stockPrices.lower(150));   // 120

        // Range slice
        System.out.println("Range [120..180]: " + stockPrices.subSet(120, true, 180, true));
    }
}
```

**Console Output:**
```text
Sorted Prices: [105, 120, 150, 180, 210]
First (Min):   105
Last (Max):    210
Ceiling >= 140: 150
Floor <= 140:   120
Higher > 150:   180
Lower < 150:    120
Range [120..180]: [120, 150, 180]
```

---

### Critical Difference: HashSet vs TreeSet Equality

| Dimension | `HashSet<E>` | `TreeSet<E>` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Ordering** | Unordered (random hash buckets) | Sorted (Natural or Comparator) |
| **Uniqueness Mechanism** | `equals()` and `hashCode()` | `compareTo()` or `compare() == 0` |
| **Add / Contains Cost** | Amortized $O(1)$ | Guaranteed $O(\log N)$ |
| **Null Elements** | Allows 1 null | Throws `NullPointerException` on insert |

questions.question: How does TreeSet evaluate whether two objects are duplicates?
options: By checking if comparator.compare(o1, o2) == 0 (or o1.compareTo(o2) == 0)
By checking reference identity o1 == o2
questions.explanation: TreeSet relies strictly on its sorting mechanism (Comparable.compareTo or Comparator.compare). If compare(a, b) == 0, the elements are treated as duplicates, even if a.equals(b) would return false!

questions.question: What is the time complexity of set.add(), set.contains(), and set.remove() in a TreeSet?
questions.explanation: Because a Red-Black Tree guarantees that the tree height is balanced and never exceeds 2 * log2(N + 1), search, insertion, and deletion all run in strictly guaranteed O(log N) time.

questions.question: What happens when set.add(null) is executed on a default TreeSet in Java?
options: The null is placed at the root of the tree
The null is stored as a special EMPTY node
questions.explanation: TreeSet must compare the inserted element with existing nodes. Since null.compareTo() cannot be called, a NullPointerException is thrown.

questions.question: What is the difference between ceiling(e) and higher(e) in NavigableSet?
options: ceiling(e) returns >= e (inclusive); higher(e) returns > e (strictly exclusive)
ceiling(e) returns <= e; higher(e) returns >= e
ceiling(e) throws an exception if an exact match is missing
questions.explanation: ceiling(e) returns the least element greater than OR EQUAL to e. higher(e) returns the least element STRICTLY GREATER than e.

questions.question: Explain the major bug that occurs if compareTo() is inconsistent with equals() in TreeSet.
questions.answer: If compareTo() is inconsistent with equals() (e.g., compareTo returns 0 for two objects where equals() returns false), TreeSet will reject the second object as a duplicate and fail to insert it. For example, if a Student class compares only by grade in compareTo(), two different students with the same grade cannot both exist in a TreeSet! In contrast, HashSet will insert both students because their equals() returns false. To avoid bugs, compareTo() must be strictly consistent with equals().

questions.question: What happens if you insert an object that does not implement Comparable into a default new TreeSet()?
questions.answer: When the second element is inserted (or when the first element is checked against the root in modern Java), the JVM attempts to cast the object to java.lang.Comparable. Because the class does not implement Comparable and no custom Comparator was supplied, the JVM throws a java.lang.ClassCastException at runtime.

questions.question: How does TreeSet subSet() differ from creating a new filtered set?
questions.answer: TreeSet.subSet(from, to) returns a backed 'view' of the original tree, not a deep copy. Mutations to the original set within the range are immediately visible in the subSet view, and mutations made to the subSet write directly into the backing TreeSet. Attempting to insert an element into the subSet outside its bounded range throws an IllegalArgumentException.
